claim: Human learners show an aptitude-treatment crossover: high-assistance (worked examples, integrated text, narration) helps low-prior-knowledge learners and low-assistance helps high-prior-knowledge learners.
agent_test: Split task classes by measured pass rate; randomise lesson on or off inside each band; compare pass rate at equal tokens. Expect a positive gap in weak classes and a zero or negative gap in strong classes.
audit_note: Kalyuga 2007 (existence/title verified via Crossref; content is the standard expertise-reversal review) and Leppink et al. 2011 (interaction F(3,97)=2.762, d=0.96/1.06) verified; note in Leppink the high-prior advantage of arguments over worked examples was not significant (d=0.51), so the 'crossover' is partly a pattern, not a significant reversal.

claim: The pooled human effect is moderate and asymmetric: d = +0.505 for assistance in low-knowledge groups, d = -0.428 for withholding assistance in high-knowledge groups (60 studies, 176 effects, 5924 participants). Help for novices is worth more than removing help from experts. Full text now read: heterogeneity is very high (I2 90.87% and 87.55%), Egger tests are not significant (p=.57, .77), and the difference of differences is d = 0.971 (CI 0.631 to 1.312), below the 1.72 of the 2007 review. Measured (median-split) knowledge groups show only about -0.2 on the expert side.
agent_test: Budget expectations: removing lessons on strong classes should gain only a small amount; the main saving is tokens, not accuracy. Test token saving at equal pass rate.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Many human reversals are partial: the interaction is significant but the expert-side effect is not, or novice benefit simply vanishes. Clean sign flips are the minority.
agent_test: Gate rule should be 'drop the lesson when the class is strong' (safe even when neutral), not 'invert the lesson'. Check on the agent that dropping loses nothing on strong classes.
audit_note: Only the Kalyuga (2007) abstract/reference list was reachable (full text paywalled; no text on partial vs full reversals) and the Tetzlaff 2025 PDF host (pedocs) refused connection, so Table 3 numbers and the 'partial reversals more common' statement could not be checked; b19 and b20 are also the same Kalyuga paper.

claim: Worked-example benefit shrinks as prior knowledge rises and can reverse for the most knowledgeable learners (e.g., a crossover in first-year statistics, Leppink et al. 2011); a three-step gradient (retention plus transfer / retention only / none) is not supported by the sources checked.
agent_test: Use at least three bands (weak, middle, strong) by class pass rate rather than one threshold. Compare full lesson, shortened lesson and none per band.
audit_note: Leppink 2011 verified (crossover, numbers match) but shows a crossover not a graded retention/transfer gradient; Chen thesis host unreachable and its listed finding says the effect reversed for the most knowledgeable group, not 'none'; the retention-only/middle tier is not in any listed finding.
claim_before_audit: Reversal is graded, not a switch: worked-example benefit shrinks stepwise as prior knowledge rises (none for most expert, retention only for middle, retention plus transfer for least).

claim: The same material flips sign within a single learner population as skill rises over weeks (longitudinal designs, d from +1.67 to -0.44; same children flip within 2 weeks). Numbers come from one review table; two agents transcribed it, so this is one source, not two.
agent_test: A lesson's value must be re-measured as the class record changes. Rerun the gate after each batch of tasks; do not freeze a lesson-on list.

claim: Fading (removing solution steps gradually) improves near transfer and reduces errors during learning over example-problem pairs, but far transfer gains are not reliable. Adding prompts to name the principle for each step gives medium to large effects on both. A later large study found no fading advantage (see K07).
agent_test: On a mid-skill class compare: full lesson, lesson with last step removed plus 'name the rule', bare problem. Equal tokens, near and far item sets.

claim: Fading did not beat example-problem pairs in a large eighth-grade study (N=143); example-first order was the only reliable contrast, and prior knowledge was the strongest predictor.
agent_test: Do not assume fading is better than plain example-first. Treat fading as optional; include an example-first arm as a control.

claim: In one study of legal case reasoning (a less structured task), worked examples beat problem solving for both first-year and third-year law students, so no expertise reversal appeared even though third-years had much more prior knowledge; generalisation to art history or literature is not shown.
agent_test: Skill band must be defined per task class and by the agent's own schema coverage, not by general capability. In open-ended classes keep lessons even for a strong model; test with a class where pass rate is high but the task is ill-defined.
audit_note: Nievelstein et al. 2013 verified (numbers match; first- and third-year law students both benefited from worked examples) but it covers law only, not art history or literature; the Chen geometry thesis (unreachable) is not an ill-structured domain; 'because students lack the key schema' is interpretation, and the third-year students had much more prior knowledge (d=2.75).
claim_before_audit: Expertise reversal fails to appear in ill-structured domains (law, art history, literature) because students still lack the key schema: worked examples beat problem solving for both year groups.

claim: Element interactivity is a better predictor than topic label: expertise folds interacting elements into one schema, so guidance becomes redundant only for items with few remaining interacting elements.
agent_test: Predict lesson value by item complexity (number of interacting steps) as well as class pass rate. Test whether item-level step count adds predictive power over class pass rate.

claim: Delayed tests can reveal effects that immediate tests miss (trigonometry: no interaction immediately, significant interaction after a week; Cognitive Tutor classroom: adaptive fading won only on the delayed test).
agent_test: Score lessons on held-out items in a later session (fresh item set, new context) as well as in-session. Without delay the agent cannot show retention at all.
audit_note: Chen (2016) thesis is behind an SSO login (the trigonometry immediate-vs-delayed interaction could not be checked); only the Cognitive Tutor half was confirmed, second-hand, through Kalyuga's 2010 editorial summary of Salden et al. (adaptive fading won on delayed but not immediate classroom posttest), not the Salden paper itself.

claim: Adapting guidance to a measured skill level beats non-adapted sequences (effect sizes 0.46 to 0.69 across several studies); the exact adaptation rule matters little.
agent_test: Compare a cheap gate (3 to 5 held-out probes, pass-rate threshold) against random and always-on lessons at equal tokens. Several rule variants should tie.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: A rapid first-step or step-verification probe predicts full-test skill (r up to .92, .71, .75) while cutting test time 3.2 to 4.9 times, but only on well-defined tasks.
agent_test: Check whether the first-step pass rate of the agent on 3 items predicts the full class pass rate on 20 items; report correlation and token cost.

claim: Short training can create the effect: a brief prior session flips the sign on added text, so even modest prior exposure to a class changes which format helps.
agent_test: Check whether the lesson effect flips after the agent has solved only a few items of the class in its own context (in-run exposure).
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Support stays useful for everyone when the task load is very high (icons helped all with three parameters at once). The table entry for the novice effect in that study is probably mistyped (see critique).
agent_test: Include a very hard band. Do not drop lessons on hard items even when the class pass rate is high.

claim: In agent loops, a curated skill document raises pass rate on average (SkillsBench 33.9% to 50.5%, +16.6 pp, 18 configurations, 87 tasks; re-opened and confirmed), but gains differ widely (+4.1 to +25.7 pp) and 13 of 87 tasks got worse (worst -7.4 pp).
agent_test: Per-class paired design: same tasks with and without the lesson, report per-class delta, and the share of classes where the lesson hurts. Use as the basis for the gate.

claim: Model-written lessons hurt: self-generated skills fell 8.1 to 11.5 pp below no skills on all three tested configurations (SkillsBench, re-opened). Unfiltered agent-induced task-level skills also lowered average success in a second study (-1.2 pp text, -4.1 pp code over 11 models, 3 benchmarks). Causes audited: the solver never opens the skill, authoring uses up the trial, confident wrong content, leakage.
agent_test: Test lessons written by the agent against lessons written from verified failing outputs at equal tokens, per step type rather than per whole task. Keep only verified lessons. Writer strength matters little (d21); the gate matters.
audit_note: Minor: the -1.2/-4.1 pp averages in Feng et al. have overlapping CIs and the SkillsBench Claude Code self-generated runs used higher effort than baseline; neither changes the claim.

claim: Compact lessons beat exhaustive ones: compact +19.0, standard +21.5, detailed +14.5, comprehensive +0.7 pp; 4 or more skills per task +10.1 vs +18.0 to +19.0 for 1 to 3.
agent_test: Cap lesson length (for example one line) and number shown per task (1 to 3). Test one line vs paragraph vs three lessons at equal total tokens.
audit_note: All numbers come from the single SkillsBench paper (Honda cheat-sheet paper is a different setting and gives no support for the skill-length numbers); comprehensive bucket has only 5 tasks and buckets are observational, not an ablation.

claim: A worked example added inside a medium-guidance skill gives no detectable gain on average (+0.7 pp GPT-5.5, +1.3 pp DeepSeek V4-Flash, CIs include zero; the study could only detect 8.3 to 16.0 pp). The test was not split by competence.
agent_test: Rerun the example vs no-example contrast within competence bands with enough tasks; the average null may hide a crossover.

claim: Skill documents help most where pretraining is thin and least where it is strong (math and operations research +9.7 pp, among the lowest). This is the domain-level analogue of reversal, not a within-task-class test. Counter-check: across 18 SkillsBench configurations the lift is unrelated to the no-skill pass rate (r = -0.03, computed from Table 2), so a model-level reversal is not seen there.
agent_test: Use the base model's zero-shot pass rate per class as the competence measure; correlate it with lesson gain across classes.

claim: More examples can hurt LLMs: many-shot returns are non-monotone, harder tasks degrade at shorter contexts, and for strong models few shots suffice. On MATH500 (Gemini 1.5 Pro) 8-shot 86.3, 400-shot 82.3, cheat sheet 88.0 (re-opened and confirmed).
agent_test: Sweep number of lessons (0, 1, 3, 10) per class and look for a hump; pick the number by class pass rate.
audit_note: Honda MATH500 numbers (Gemini 1.5 Pro 86.3/82.3/88.0), Agarwal MATH/GPQA decline after 125 shots and Zou harder-tasks-degrade-earlier all match; the 'few shots suffice for strong models' part rests on a GPT-4.1 figure whose values were not read.

claim: The harm from demonstrations falls with model strength: small models are damaged by shifted but correct demonstrations (Llama-2-7B 96.4 to 56.9 at 100% shifted; Llama-3.1-8B 98.2 to 66.0); strong recent models stay within about 2%. Llama-2-70B is an exception (97.3 to 87.6, SD 11.8). The shift is a style change of the inputs, not knowledge-redundant examples.
agent_test: Competence threshold should be per model: the same lesson library may need gating differently for a small and a large model. Repeat the gate on two model sizes.
audit_note: All numbers verified in Qiu et al. 2026, but every cited line is the same single preprint (one lab), so the model-strength trend is not independently replicated; 'style change not knowledge-redundant' is the paper's perturbation design, accurately characterised.

claim: Models that already reason well can be hurt by examples or by forced step-by-step: the DeepSeek-R1 report says few-shot degrades it (statement only, no table); CoT gives small gains for reasoning models and makes some models worse on questions they always got right (Gemini Flash 2.0 -0.131 on the 100%-correct metric).
agent_test: Compare lesson-on vs lesson-off on items the agent already passes 100% of the time; count regressions.

claim: Chain-of-thought gains concentrate in math and symbolic tasks (+14.2 symbolic, +12.3 math, +6.9 logical; other categories 56.8 vs 56.1; 110 papers, 1,218 comparisons; re-opened and confirmed).
agent_test: Gate extra reasoning by task type, as part of the same competence gate.

claim: Learning to choose the amount of thinking by difficulty cuts length with no loss: AdaptThink 1.5B, GSM8K 83.1 vs 79.0, average +2.4 points and -53.0% length, NoThinking used on 86.9% of GSM8K vs 40.4% of AIME24 (re-opened and confirmed).
agent_test: Closest machine analogue of fading support by competence. Compare a code-run difficulty router against uniform budget at equal tokens.

claim: LLM-as-expert-evaluator reproduces the ordinal expertise reversal pattern for simulated students (120 personas: worked > practice for low expertise, no difference for high), but LLMs cannot be made to play a stable novice, so such simulations are not human evidence.
agent_test: Do not use LLM-simulated learners to tune the gate; use real agent runs on held-out items.

claim: Over-help is a failure mode in AI tutors and with unrestricted AI help: Socratic tutors drift to giving the answer under pressure; unrestricted AI helped novices produce code but 77% failed a no-AI maintenance task vs 39% for scaffolded.
agent_test: Not a direct agent test (human learners with AI tutors). Relevant only as design caution: a lesson that gives the answer undermines the attempt.

claim: LLM-generated faded examples gave no significant cognitive-load advantage over standard feedback for 27 teaching assistants; only a search summary was seen.
agent_test: No direct test; skip unless full text found.

claim: Prior knowledge did not predict who benefited from LLM access in a randomised self-study; skill at using the AI did (treatment x pre-exam p=0.2, three-way with AI competence p<.05).
agent_test: Human study of AI use, not a test of lessons for an agent. Cautions that gains may depend on how the lesson is used, not only on prior skill.

claim: No published study found tests expertise reversal of lessons for a language-model agent with a within-class competence split at equal tokens. The closest are cross-cell correlations (agent-written skills: rho -0.55 and -0.45 over 33 cells) and one same-harness two-model comparison (+66.7 vs +5.6).
agent_test: This is the experiment to run: bands by class pass rate x lesson on/off x equal tokens x two model sizes.
audit_note: Cortex +66.7 vs +5.6 (Haiku 4.5 vs Sonnet 5, CI of the 5.6 spans zero) and Feng rho -0.55/-0.45 over 33 cells verified; the 'no published study found' part is an absence claim that cannot be proven by sources, and Xu&Wu/SkillsBench do not test the split.

claim: Agent-written task-level lessons help mainly where the no-memory baseline is very low, and the benefit shrinks as the baseline rises: Spearman rho = -0.55 (text) and -0.45 (code) over 33 model-benchmark cells (p < 0.05); GPT-OSS-120B on AppWorld fell from 27.3 to 17.0 (text) and 1.0 (code). Closest agent analogue of expertise reversal, but across cells, not within a class.
agent_test: Within-class test: same tasks, lesson on/off, bands by zero-shot pass rate of the class, paired, 3 or more seeds (d26).

claim: The benefit of a lesson or harness is hump-shaped in model strength, not a straight decline: on SWE-bench Verified gains are +4.4 (3.6% base), +19.3 (20.7%), +15.8 (26.2%), then +2.4 to +2.8 for 66% to 74% bases. The weakest models often do not load the lesson (25% load rate) or follow it (0.142 following rate).
agent_test: Gate needs a floor as well as a ceiling. Measure lesson load rate and following rate per class; below a floor, spend tokens on something else (a worked example near the point of use, or a stronger model).

claim: Strong models already ignore lessons selectively: Claude Opus 4.6 read the skill file in about 20% of default runs vs 48% average; forced reading raises use to 94% but steps are still skipped or contradicted. Stronger models also ignore irrelevant retrieved skills better than weaker ones, which fall to or below no-skill (Kimi 19.8 vs 21.8, Qwen 19.7 vs 20.5).
agent_test: Offer lessons as an optional lookup for strong classes, forced for weak classes; compare accuracy and tokens.
audit_note: Numbers match OpenSkillEval (48%, Opus 4.6 ~20%, 94%) and Liu et al. (Kimi 19.8 vs 21.8, Qwen 19.7 vs 20.5); 'stronger models ignore irrelevant skills better' rests on three models (Opus, Kimi, Qwen), gaps of 0.8 to 2.0 pp with no significance test, and is the authors' interpretation.

claim: Harmful skills are mostly relevant ones that make the agent build or verify too much, not irrelevant ones: of 307 skill-induced failures, 68.8% of functional failures were implementation faults, only 1.6% applicability mismatch; 62.6% of efficiency regressions were excessive procedure. SkillsBench shows the same: a skill displaces a stronger native strategy on some tasks.
agent_test: Add an applicability boundary and a light fast path to each lesson; drop the lesson when the class already passes.

claim: In one terminal-task benchmark an unfiltered self-evolving skill pool peaked at round 3 and ended only 2 points above round 1 (a gated pool reached 72%, 10 points above the ungated best), and removing the source skills recovered only 1.7 pp; in a separate procedurally generated code-repair stream, accepted skills applied globally scored 0.713 vs 0.775 for no edits, while the same skills scoped to their originating task family scored 0.816.
agent_test: Gate every new lesson with a paired with/without check before it enters the pool; scope by task class; cap pool size.
audit_note: Numbers verified in Shang et al. (peak R3, +2 at R5, 72%, +10 over best ungated, 1.7 pp) and Cheng et al. (0.713, 0.775, 0.816), but 'Lessons must be scoped' generalises from one procedurally generated 12-round code-repair benchmark with fixed family conventions (eight streams), and the two results are single preprints from different setups.
claim_before_audit: An unfiltered, self-evolving lesson pool rises to a peak and then falls (Terminal-Bench 2: ungated peak at round 3, only +2 at round 5; gated pool reaches 72%, 10 points above the ungated best), and removing the bad source skills recovers little (1.7 pp). Lessons must be scoped to their task family: global memory 0.713 vs no-edit 0.775; same skills scoped 0.816.

claim: Few probe items give an unstable class pass rate: with 5 items and a true rate of 0.7 the chance of observing at least 0.8 is 0.53; the Wilson 95% interval for 10 items at 50% is [0.24, 0.76]. About 20 or more items are needed for plus or minus 0.2. A paired with/without evidence count of about six states per skill reached the plateau in one agent study, with failure at 1 to 4.
agent_test: Use a smoothed class estimate and a wide middle band. Default classes with fewer than about 6 to 10 paired states to the middle band. Calculation is mine; the SkillApt plateau is one study.

claim: Detecting a 5 pp lesson effect inside a class needs about 560 to 1570 unpaired trials per arm (141 to 392 for 10 pp); a paired design with seeds is needed. Existing agent studies (30 to 87 tasks) can only detect about 8 to 17 pp.
agent_test: Plan the first S0 test on 20 or more classes of 30 or more items, paired, 3 or more seeds, and report per-class deltas with intervals.

claim: In humans, measured (median-split) knowledge groups show a weaker reversal than groups defined by grade level: high-knowledge estimate about -0.21 for measured groups and -0.20 for intervention groups vs -0.95 for grade level (dummy-coded Table 3, offsets added by me). Moderation by assessment type explains R2 = 50% on the expert side.
agent_test: Our competence band comes from a measured pass rate, which is the weak case. Expect a small expert-side effect and plan the token saving, not accuracy, as the main gain.
